summary: The bill amends 18 U.S.C. 922 to make it unlawful for any person in the business of destroying firearms to fail to destroy every component of a firearm shipped in interstate or foreign commerce, expands the definition of 'engaged in the business' to cover such destroyers, and adds penalties of fines, up to 2 years imprisonment, and license suspension or revocation.

scores.thoughts: The bill amends criminal statutes related to firearm destruction practices and adds penalties for violations. It contains no provisions related to federal spending, appropriations, or budget allocations.
The bill makes no changes to tax law, rates, deductions, or revenue collection mechanisms.
No provisions address healthcare policy, insurance, public health programs, or medical services.

The bill adds a new prohibition under 18 U.S.C. § 922(aa) requiring complete destruction of all firearm components by commercial destroyers, expands the statutory definition of 'engaged in the business' to cover firearm destroyers, and imposes criminal penalties plus potential license revocation. This constitutes a new regulatory requirement on firearm handling and disposal, directly advancing stricter gun-related rules.
The legislation has no connection to immigration, border policy, visas, or related enforcement.
No provisions relate to reproductive rights, abortion access, or restrictions.
The bill does not address military budgets, defense procurement, or armed forces policy.
No environmental, regulatory, or climate-related content appears in the bill.

The legislation does not address controlled substances, decriminalization, or drug enforcement.

The bill creates a new federal misdemeanor/felony violation with up to two years imprisonment and license sanctions for improper firearm destruction. While this adds to criminal penalties, the change is narrowly technical and ancillary to the primary gun-destruction purpose.
No trade, tariff, or import/export policy provisions exist.
